findings.what: The folded-in javadoc claims "the seal depends on a losing writer treating its loss as proof it is fenced, and {@code commit} does the opposite by construction, folding the winner's offsets in and retrying at the next sequence forever". That is contradicted by this same file's commit(): lines 249-266 test `taken instanceof Seal` and `throw fenced(seal)` -- commit fails CLOSED on a lost slot that turns out to be a SEAL, and has done since M4.5 (its own comment there says so). The true reason the epoch-0 chain cannot be sealed is the next sentence, "there is no leader there to fence": LocalSequencer.start only seals when `prevEpoch >= 1`, so nothing ever writes a SEAL into epoch 0's prefix. The prose is carried over verbatim from the deleted constructor's javadoc (and from the M4.6/M4.6d backlog rows), but this commit is what makes it permanent on the surviving constructor.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader of the surviving constructor's javadoc concludes that CommitLog.commit folds a SEAL in and keeps writing past the barrier, and either adds a redundant fencing guard in a caller or, worse, treats I5 ("no acknowledged commit exists beyond a SEAL in its own chain") as not held by commit and weakens the assertion in CommitLogTest/CommitLogSealTest that pins it.

findings.what: Production comment left naming the deleted constructor: "the reserved unleased chain, which every `CommitLog(store, prefix)` uses". After this commit that expression does not compile and nothing uses epoch 0 by default. The deletion is otherwise complete at the call sites but not in the prose that documents why the epoch-0 branch in replayAncestry exists.
findings.failure_scenario: A future reader of replayAncestry looks for the `CommitLog(store, prefix)` callers this comment says exist, finds none, and concludes the `hops.add(new Hop(epoch, upTo))` line before the `chainEpoch >= 1` loop is dead defensive code for a caller that no longer exists -- and removes it, which is the exact regression the comment records (an epoch-0 log recovering NOTHING) and which no test in the tree would catch once no epoch-0 chain is recovered.

findings.what: Two comments still assert the deleted default exists: line 75 "`CommitLog`'s 2-arg constructor writes epoch 0 for every caller that has no lease yet -- `DefaultIngest` among them" (false since M4.6d for DefaultIngest, false since this commit for the constructor) and line 469 "a lease at epoch 0 would collide with `CommitLog`'s no-lease default". These are the reasoning that justifies theFirstAcquisitionStartsAtEpochOneBecauseZeroMeansNoLease and noAcquisitionEverWritesEpochZeroBecauseItIsReservedForTheUnleasedChain, so they are the prose most likely to be read when someone asks whether M4.4b's reservation is still needed.
findings.failure_scenario: An agent revisiting M4.4b reads these comments, verifies that neither the 2-arg constructor nor a DefaultIngest caller exists, concludes the reservation of epoch 0 is obsolete, and changes LeaseManager's cold start to mint epoch 0 -- which re-opens the I3 hole (a first leader's chain byte-identical to the historical unleased one, so "readers of the new epoch never look there" is void) and simultaneously breaks CONTINUE's prevEpoch==0 "no predecessor" sentinel that ChainReplay.inherited and replayAncestry both gate on.
